body:
### Problem

Currently, if you have a buffer like
```
line1
line2
line3
```
And you place a cursor on the first two lines with
```
QjQj
```
Then you have two multicursors, and one normal cursor. But if you do `[C`, the cursor on the last line disappears.

### Expected behavior

The main cursor would be treated more like a multicursor, and so when we left the current position, a cursor would be left behind.

Perhaps the main cursor actually _should_ be a multicursor, and when reading from the nvim.multicursor namespace, it would be included with some data (`{ primary = true }`). This would mean the namespace would never be empty, but you could still gate on multiple cursors by checking if the returned table has length `> 1`. For plugins that do multicursor stuff, this might make behavior more intuitive.

That's not necessary, for the record, and could be moved to a separate issue. Just thinking out loud.

comment_data.body:
> so when we left the current position, a cursor would be left behind

don't know how to make sense of that, since every motion "leaves the current position".





> Perhaps the main cursor actually _should_ be a multicursor, and when reading from the nvim.multicursor namespace, it would be included with some data (`{ primary = true }`)

it's enticing. but the first problem is that the primary cursor is window-relative: every window showing the same buffer, has its own cursor. whereas multicursors are buffer-relative.

also it ends up requiring special handling everywhere, and i'm not aware of any use-cases where it simplifies things enough to offset that.

> don't know how to make sense of that, since every motion "leaves the current position".

I mean "leave" as in "deposit" - place a multicursor where we just left our main cursor. `QjQj` only places two multicursors, and so when you use `[C`, the third line has no cursor on it anymore. But I would expect my primary cursor to just be "one of the cursors", rather than needing _another_ `Q` to be run before I leave.

> and so when you use `[C`, the third line has no cursor on it anymore.

but you didn't hit `Q` there... if you do, then everything will work. it won't "double" the operations; if the primary cursor overlaps a cursor, it counts as 1 total cursor.

that's a very obvious model for users to understand. whereas, i'm not really sure how it would be obvious which motions "deposit" a cursor behind them. that seems confusing...

I think the point is that for multicursor users "go to next cursor" is interpreted as/a less desirable command than "make the next cursor the primary one", i.e. they expect/want "go to next cursor" to not "decrease" the amount of cursors, ever.
Otherwise `[C` decreases the amount of cursor on the first time, but not on the second input, i.e. it acts 'differently' on repeat inputs,
which is confusing.

I understand the reasoning for the new behavior of `[C`. However, this change of behavior doesn't leave an easy way to delete a cursor I misplaced. Before, I was able to delete cursors by pressing `[CQ` repeatedly. With the current change, a new cursor would be created after each `[C` and it would undo the previous deletion. I think either this change should be reverted or a new mapping should be added for just navigating between cursors without placing a new cursor.

I do think that a mapping to delete a cursor would make more sense than reverting the mapping.
In the meantime I did post a function that 'deletes' the current cursor and places you on the closest one in #41895, if you'd like,
though it's not quite robust around duplicate cursors.

@Xmgplays is your implemention replicating the previous behavior of `[C`?

In my understanding, the previous behavior was very precise with a minor inconsistency when navigating away from current cursor. This inconsistency can easily fixed by pressing `Q` before the movement. I get how this can annoy people.

However, without the old behavior we lose the use case for just navigating between cursors without placing new ones. If your new implementation always deletes the current cursor when moving, it has complicated the matter even further.

If I want to delete the current cursor, I can press `Q`. With a placement motion and a deletion motion, we would have split up the former precise behavior into two imprecise and more complex behaviors.

Compare this: deletion of the 4th last cursor without placing a cursor at the current position and moving back to the latest cursor - I assume `[X` to be the new deletion motion
- `[X2[C]X2]C` new behavior with placing/deletion movements
- `3[CQ2]C` old behavior

To me, motions that place additional cursors introduce the requirement to think more. While I know that if I mess up a simple movement I can simply undo it with `<C-o>`, while a motion that adds cursors requires `<C-o>Q`.

I guess, I'm just in love with the simple and precise original behavior and wish someone brought it back.

@justinmk what do you suggest as a next step to restore the ability to do a pure navigation between cursors so that cursors can be deleted again? I'd be happy to create/support a PR that restores the original behavior under a different mapping.

> the previous behavior was very precise with a minor inconsistency when navigating away from current cursor. This inconsistency can easily fixed by pressing `Q` before the movement

makes sense. if we can provide a mapping example that satisfies the "leave a cursor" behavior, it's better for the default behavior to be simple. "leaving a cursor behind" is indeed surprising.

One thing I'd note is that I don't know of any other system, that works the way the old `[C` mappings work. Neither helix, nor multicursor.nvim work that way and I'm not sure any other multicursor interface has such a mapping, which to me suggest that that behavior *is* surprising.

I also don't really see a case where the old behavior is actually useful, since even in the example @jceb mentioned, why do you care whether you left a cursor behind or not, if you are jumping back there later anyway. There is no difference between `[X3[C[X2]C` and just `3[C[X2[C`. Overall I do think that the current behavior is a more intuitive interface, even if it's not the most basic version. 

Anyway I'm not too particular about all of this, since I can get my desired behavior anyway, but something I'd like to mention at the end: the inconsistency of the old `]C` mappings could not be fixed by simply pressing `Q` beforehand, since that has unexpected behavior depending on if the current position is a duped cursor or not. Which could easily occur with the way that the current `{count}Q`, `v_{count}Q` and `Q` mappings.

> why do you care whether you left a cursor behind or not, if you are jumping back there later anyway

That's not always the case.

Nvim multicursor is designed to treat mcursors as *marks*. It is very much intended that you can explore the rest of the buffer, or other buffers, or whatever, and return later to continue working with multicursors. Thus if I hit `G` to go to EOB temporarily, then returning to the cursors with `[C`, there is no reason to assume I want to add a cursor at EOB.



> Neither helix, nor multicursor.nvim work

Other multicursor impls are much less fleixble. Nvim mcursor is intended to be maximally flexible but also very intuitive/ergonomic. I don't think this one difference is a sign of "unintuitiveness" (actually the contrary), so mimicking other editors/IDEs isn't relevant here.



> the old `]C` mappings could not be fixed by simply pressing `Q` beforehand

We will probably need to support something like `1Q` which forces a cursor instead of "toggling".
Yes, `1Q` would be awesome as well as `0Q` to ensure a cursor exists / doesn't exist at the current position.

I guess that ends up being a difference in how I use/want to use multicursors and what you are imagining. As a toolkit to build upon I think your vision works out well, but I still think the other way around makes for a better out-of-the-box experience.
Anyway either way is fine for me personally, so do what you think makes sense as a default.

Also agree on something like `1Q` to force a cursor and something else to delete/'unforce' a/multiple cursors(and maybe someway to dedupe cursors as well, not necessarily a binding).
@justinmk should we reopen this issue or how shall we proceed?

i'll address it soon

> but I still think the other way around makes for a better out-of-the-box experience

I don't really accept that. Leaving side-effects (except the `'` mark) behind when you jump, is contrary to (1) other jumps in Nvim, (2) other jumps in multicursor. 

It might appear that helix/etc "work" that way because they just don't even have a way to move a primary cursor independently.
